status: Draft from the mishnah and Kehati, under review.

mishnayot.title: The ox, the cow and the calf: before or after?
mishnayot.summary: When it is unclear whether the calf was lost because of the goring, the owner pays a quarter of its value, half of the disputed half.

b: A harmless ox gored a cow and killed it, and its newborn calf was found beside her.
Mishnah 5:1
It is not known whether she gave birth before the goring or because of it.
Mishnah 5:1
For the cow: half damages, as for any harmless ox.
Mishnah 5:1
For the calf: a quarter damages. If the goring caused the loss of the calf he would owe half damages for it, if not, nothing; the money in doubt is divided.
Kehati 5:1
A cow gored an ox and a living newborn is found beside her, and it is not known whether she gave birth before the goring: half damages from the cow and a quarter damages from the newborn.
Mishnah 5:1

If the cow is there, half damages is collected from her; if she is gone, a quarter damages is collected from the calf's own body, since it is doubtful whether the calf's strength helped in the goring.
Kehati 5:1
The mishnah follows Sumchus, who divides money that is in doubt.
Kehati 5:1

This mishnah follows the view of Sumchus that money in doubt is split. The Gemara cites the Sages, who say the one who wants the money must bring proof, and the halakha follows the Sages: if he cannot prove that the goring caused the loss of the calf, nothing is paid for the calf.
Kehati 5:1

picture: The ox gored the cow, and her calf is found dead beside her. Did she give birth before or after? The ox's owner pays half for the cow and a quarter for the calf.

mishnayot.title: Pots and produce in someone else's courtyard
mishnayot.summary: If you bring your things into a courtyard without permission, the householder is not liable for damage to them. With permission, he is.

b: A potter brought his pots into a householder's courtyard without permission and the householder's cattle broke them: the householder is not liable.
Mishnah 5:2
If the cattle were injured by the pots, the owner of the pots is liable.
Mishnah 5:2
The householder could say: who gave you permission to bring them in?
Kehati 5:2
If he brought them in by permission and the cattle broke them, the owner of the courtyard is liable. [By giving permission he is taken to have accepted to guard them.]
Mishnah 5:2; Kehati 5:2
Likewise, if his things injured the householder's cattle, the visitor is exempt, since guarding them is the householder's job.
Kehati 5:2
The same applies to a man who brought produce into the courtyard and the cattle ate it.
Mishnah 5:2
The householder is liable for what his cattle do to the visitor's things only if he accepted to guard them. The halakha follows Rabbi (5:3).
Kehati 5:3
If the cattle ate so much of the produce that they died, the owner of the produce is exempt, since the animal should not have eaten so much.
Kehati 5:2

mishnayot.title: A man brings his ox into a courtyard
mishnayot.summary: The same rules as the last mishnah, applied to a visiting ox, plus a cistern and the view of Rabbi.

b: If the householder's ox gored the visiting ox, or the householder's dog bit it, the householder is not liable.
Mishnah 5:3
If the visiting ox gored the householder's ox, its owner is liable.
Mishnah 5:3
If the visiting ox fell into the cistern and fouled its water, its owner is liable.
Mishnah 5:3
If the householder's father or son was in the cistern and the ox fell in and killed him, the ox's owner pays the ransom (kofer).
Mishnah 5:3
The owner of the courtyard is liable.
Mishnah 5:3
Rabbi: in all of these the householder is not liable until he accepts to guard. Permission to enter does not by itself make him the guard of the visitor's things.
Mishnah 5:3; Kehati 5:3
The halakha follows Rabbi: letting someone in does not make the householder liable for his things; only if he accepted to guard them.
Kehati 5:3

The ox that fell into the cistern and killed the householder's father or son: the Gemara speaks of an ox that was an attested danger to fall on people. It is exempt from death, since it did not intend to kill, but its owner pays the ransom (kofer).
Kehati 5:3

The mishnah says "his father or son" only as an example; the same holds for any other person. Kehati gives the view that Rabbi Yose HaGelili and Rabbi Tarfon, who hold that damage in the injured party's domain is paid in full, are the source for a full kofer here.
Kehati 5:3

mishnayot.title: An ox or a man strikes a woman and she miscarries
mishnayot.summary: A man who causes a miscarriage pays for the offspring; an ox's owner does not. (This mishnah deals with a sensitive subject; the picture below is a diagram only.)

b: An ox that aimed at another ox and struck a woman, and her children came out: its owner does not pay for the offspring.
Mishnah 5:4
A man who aimed at another man and struck a woman: he pays for the offspring.
Mishnah 5:4
The payment for offspring comes from the verse about men who fight (Exodus 21:22), so it applies to a person and not to an ox, even if the ox aimed at the woman.
Kehati 5:4
The first view: they assess the woman's value before she gave birth and after.
Mishnah 5:4

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: then a woman who gives birth would be worth more after, since childbirth endangers her. Instead they assess what the offspring would be worth, and the payment is given to the husband.
Mishnah 5:4; Kehati 5:4
The payment goes to the husband, or to his heirs if he is no longer living.
Mishnah 5:4

The Gemara limits Rabban Shimon ben Gamaliel's point to a woman giving birth for the first time, since that is dangerous. For one who has given birth before he too would assess her value before and after.
Kehati 5:4
If the woman was a bondwoman who was freed, or a convert: no payment.
Mishnah 5:4
The Gemara teaches that the ox is exempt even if it aimed at the woman, because the payment for offspring is only for a person ("men fighting").
Kehati 5:4

A freed bondwoman or convert: the mishnah speaks of a woman married to a convert or freed slave who died with no heirs. The payment has no owner, so the one who damaged keeps it. Two Gemara views (Rabba, Rav Chisda) differ on when the injury happened.
Kehati 5:4

mishnayot.title: The pit
mishnayot.summary: Whoever digs a pit is liable if an animal falls in and dies, but only if the pit is ten handbreadths deep.

b: One who digs a pit in a private domain and opens it to the public, or in the public domain, or in one private domain and opens it to another private domain: he is liable.
Mishnah 5:5
If an ox or a donkey falls into a pit dug in the public domain and dies, he is liable.
Mishnah 5:5
It makes no difference whether it is a pit, a ditch, a cave, a trench or a channel.
Mishnah 5:5
Why does the Torah say "pit"? To teach that, like a pit deep enough to kill, a hole must be ten handbreadths deep for a death; a shallower one still makes him liable for an injury.
Kehati 5:5
If an animal falls in and dies, he is not liable, since it is an accident.
Mishnah 5:5; Kehati 5:5
If the animal is only injured, he is liable for full damages, since even a shallow hole can injure.
Mishnah 5:5; Kehati 5:5
It is judged by where the opening is, not where the bottom lies. A pit dug in a private domain with its opening to the public, or the reverse, makes him liable.
Kehati 5:5 (from the Tosefta)

The Gemara disputes whether the pit's liability is only when the animal dies from the foul air of the pit or also when it dies from the blow of the fall. The halakha follows Shmuel: also from the blow. So even a pit full of pillows or straw makes the digger liable.
Kehati 5:5
The same for a mound ten handbreadths high in the public domain: if an animal strikes it and dies, he is liable; if lower, he is exempt for a death but pays full damages for an injury.
Kehati 5:5

picture: Left box: a ten-handbreadth pit, the ox died: he pays. Right box: nine handbreadths, the ox died: he does not pay.

mishnayot.title: The pit: partners, covers and what falls in
mishnayot.summary: The last partner to leave the pit uncovered is liable. Then a series of limits.

b: Two partners own a pit. The first passed and did not cover it, then the second also did not: the second is liable. If the first covered it and the second found it uncovered and did not cover it, the second is liable.
Mishnah 5:6
If it was properly covered and an ox or donkey fell in and died, he is not liable.
Mishnah 5:6
An animal that fell into the pit in front of the sound of digging: the owner is liable; behind it: not liable.
Mishnah 5:6
Kehati: "backward" means it fell outside, behind the pit; then the damage did not come from the pit itself but from the sound, which is only an indirect cause (gerama).
Kehati 5:6
Trappings (the yoke and plough of an ox, the saddle of a donkey) that break: liable for the animal, exempt for the trappings.
Mishnah 5:6; Kehati 5:6

A deaf, disoriented (shoteh) or young ox falling in: the owner is liable. A clever ox that falls by day is exempt, since it could see and be careful, and that is an accident. An ox walking at night is not so.
Mishnah 5:6; Kehati 5:6 (Baraita)
A person (boy, girl, slave or bondwoman) who falls in: the owner is not liable. The verse says "ox" and not a person.
Mishnah 5:6; Kehati 5:6
A cover counts as proper only if it can stand up to ordinary wind and weight; one that cannot is as if he did not cover it.
Kehati 5:6

mishnayot.title: An ox is just an example
mishnayot.summary: For eight laws the Torah says ox, but the rule applies to all animals, including wild animals and birds.

b: The ox is an example for the pit (Exodus 21:33), keeping away from Mount Sinai (19:13), double payment (22:3, 22:8), lost property (23:4, Deuteronomy 22:1), unloading (Exodus 23:5), muzzling (Deuteronomy 25:4), diverse kinds (Leviticus 19:19, Deuteronomy 22:10) and the Sabbath (Exodus 20:10, Deuteronomy 5:14): all animals are the same.
Kehati 5:7

outline.h: Why does it say ox or donkey?
b: The Torah spoke of the usual case: people most often use an ox or a donkey.
Kehati 5:7

Kilayim (plowing with two species): by the Torah, one is liable only if plowing and leading with two kinds one of which is pure and one impure, such as an ox and a donkey. The Rabbis forbade every two kinds.
Kehati 5:7 (citing Rambam)
